feeble

/FEE-bul/ — rhymes with beetle · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something feeble is very weak, lacking strength, power, or force.

His feeble grip could barely hold the water glass after the illness.

Worked Example

After weeks of illness, the patient's feeble grip could not hold the water glass, and it slipped from her hands.

Feeble captures not just weakness but a weakness so marked it prevents action. The grip is too lacking in strength to hold the glass—far more precise than simply saying 'weak.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

delicate: Delicate means fine and easily broken or harmed — lace, thin glass, an instrument that needs careful handling. Feeble is about strength that is nearly gone: a feeble grip or voice can barely do its job. Delicate warns that a thing could be damaged; feeble says it has almost no force.

frail: Frail describes a body grown thin, breakable, and easily hurt, usually through age or illness. Feeble points at the missing strength itself — a feeble push, grip, or voice lacks the force to do its work. A frail grandmother may still have a firm handshake; a feeble one cannot.

flimsy: Flimsy describes things that are weakly made — a flimsy shelf, a flimsy excuse — likely to give way because the material or the reasoning is thin. Feeble is about low strength or force in a body or an effort: too weak to function, not too poorly built to hold.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

vigorous: full of energy and healthy strength

robust: strong, sturdy, and hard to weaken

Where it sits · how much strength is left — faint → weak → feeble → powerless

faint vs. feeble: Faint is the mildest of the set, weaker than feeble: a faint sound or effort is barely noticeable, while feeble describes strength that has nearly given out.

weak vs. feeble: Weak is less intense than feeble — weak means lacking normal strength, while feeble means so weak as to seem helpless or even pitiful.

powerless vs. feeble: Powerless is stronger than feeble: a feeble grip still holds a little strength, but a powerless one has none left at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — feble (from Latin flēbilis)

Root — feble (from Latin flēbilis): to be wept over, lamentable — from flēre, 'to weep' (Latin, via Old French)

Put it together

Put it together: Feeble comes from Latin flēbilis, 'to be wept over' — someone so weak that their condition moved others to tears. That pitiable weakness is exactly what feeble still means: very weak, lacking strength, power, or force.

Use the root in a new word: foible

Use the root in a new word: foible: Everyone has a foible — a small, harmless weakness — and foible and feeble are two spellings of the very same Old French word for 'weak.'

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Feeble is emphatic and literary—it suggests not just weakness but weakness that affects ability to function. Weak is the plain word for general lack of strength. Use feeble when describing something so weak it can barely perform its task.
